qubit.short: The unit of quantum information. Like a bit, it ends up as 0 or 1 when measured — but before that it can be in a combination of both.
qubit.long: Physically it can be a photon, an ion held by lasers, a superconducting circuit cooled close to absolute zero or the spin of an electron.

bit.short: The unit of classical information: 0 or 1, always with a definite value, even when nobody is looking.

ket.short: Dirac's notation for quantum states. |0⟩ and |1⟩ are the basis states; |ψ⟩ is any state.

superposicao.short: A state that combines possibilities, each with an amplitude. It isn't “both at once” nor “one of the two and we don't know which”: it's a third thing, with no classical analogue.

amplitude.short: The “weight” of each possibility in a quantum state. It's a complex number: the chance of measuring that result is the square of its size (the Born rule).

fase.short: The “angle” of an amplitude. On its own it doesn't change probabilities, but it decides whether two possibilities reinforce or cancel when they interfere. In the game, the bar's color shows the phase.

medicao.short: Asking the qubit “0 or 1?”. The answer is random, with odds given by the amplitudes, and afterwards the state becomes the result obtained.

colapso.short: The popular name for what happens to the state after a measurement: it “becomes” the result. What that means physically is still debated among the interpretations of quantum mechanics.

interferencia.short: Amplitudes add up like waves: equal ones reinforce (constructive), opposite ones cancel (destructive). It's the engine of almost every quantum algorithm.

esfera-de-bloch.short: A globe where every point on the surface is a state of one qubit. The north pole is |0⟩, the south pole is |1⟩, and the equator holds the half-and-half superpositions with different phases.
esfera-de-bloch.long: Named after Felix Bloch, 1952 Nobel Prize in Physics for nuclear magnetic resonance — the basis of hospital MRI scans.

porta-quantica.short: A reversible operation on qubits. On the Bloch sphere, single-qubit gates are rotations.

porta-x.short: The quantum “NOT”: swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩. It's a 180° turn around the X axis.

porta-z.short: Flips the sign of |1⟩. It doesn't change any probability, only the phase — invisible until some interference happens.

hadamard.short: The gate that creates superposition: takes |0⟩ to |+⟩ and |1⟩ to |−⟩. Applied twice, it undoes itself.

porta-s-t.short: Rotate the phase of |1⟩ by 90° (S) and 45° (T). On the sphere, they move the state around the equator.

cnot.short: A two-qubit gate: if the control (●) is 1, it applies X to the target (⊕). With the control in superposition, it creates entanglement.

cz.short: A two-qubit gate that flips the sign of |11⟩ only. It's symmetric: it doesn't matter which one is control and which is target.

emaranhamento.short: When two or more qubits form a single state that can't be described qubit by qubit. Measurement results become correlated, at any distance.
emaranhamento.long: In the game, the arrows of entangled qubits shrink toward the center of the sphere: on its own, none of them has a definite state.

estado-de-bell.short: The four most entangled states of two qubits. The most famous: (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2.

decoerencia.short: When the environment (air, heat, light, a detector) becomes entangled with the system and “spreads” the quantum information. The superposition stops interfering and the behavior looks classical.

nao-clonagem.short: It's impossible to copy an unknown quantum state. That's why quantum cryptography catches spies and why teleportation destroys the original.

oraculo.short: A black box that answers questions about a function. In quantum algorithms, it usually “marks” answers by flipping their phase.

teletransporte.short: Transferring the state of one qubit to another, far away, using an entangled pair and two classical bits. Nothing travels faster than light, and the original is destroyed.

bb84.short: The first quantum key distribution protocol (Bennett and Brassard, 1984). A spy who measures the qubits leaves marks Alice and Bob can see.

dualidade.short: Light and matter arrive in packets (like particles), but the odds of where they land add up and cancel out (like waves).

quantum.short: From the Latin for “how much”: the smallest indivisible portion of something. In 1900, Max Planck proposed that light exchanges energy in packets — the quanta.

gato-de-cheshire-quantico.short: An effect proposed in 2013 in which, in an interferometer, weak measurements suggest a particle took one path and one of its properties (like spin) took the other — the “grin without the cat”.
gato-de-cheshire-quantico.long: Observed with neutrons in 2014 (Denkmayr et al., Nature Communications). What it says about reality is still debated.
